Santa Cruz Public Libraries New resident quick start Six things to do in your first month. None of these take long, and each one saves you a scramble later. I've lived here my whole life and still keep this list. Sign up for CruzAware It's the county's official emergency alert system. Register at cruzaware.org to get evacuation and emergency warnings by call, text, or email. Set up water service If your home is on district water, start service through the San Lorenzo Valley Water District . Accounts are set up in the property owner's name, and the district asks for at least 24 business hours of notice. Find your GreenWaste pickup day Enter your address in the GreenWaste service day lookup to see your trash, recycling, and green waste collection day. Get a library card Cards are free for California residents with photo ID and proof of address. Details are on the Santa Cruz Public Libraries card page , and the Boulder Creek branch is on West Park Avenue. Get to know the fire district The Boulder Creek Fire Protection District is at 13230 Central Avenue, office line 831-338-7222. Start on defensible space early; it matters more up here than almost anywhere. Join the community Check local events , browse the directory for local businesses and services, and keep an eye on Mountain Status when weather moves in. Trash, recycling, and green waste GreenWaste picks up. The transfer station takes the rest. Boulder Creek is unincorporated Santa Cruz County, so collection runs through the county's franchise hauler. Curbside collection GreenWaste Recovery handles trash, recycling, and green waste for unincorporated Santa Cruz County. Customer service: 831-426-2711. GreenWaste county page Your pickup day Enter your address in GreenWaste's lookup tool to see your collection day. That's also the fastest way to confirm your address is in their service area. Service day lookup Bulky items and extra pickups GreenWaste's county page lists up to three bulky item reuse collections and up to four extra set out collections per year at no additional charge. Call to schedule. Program details Self-haul: Ben Lomond Transfer Station 9835 Newell Creek Road, Ben Lomond. Posted hours: Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday 7:30 am to 3:30 pm; Wednesday 7:30 am to 2:30 pm. Household hazardous waste is accepted Thursdays 7:30 am to 3:30 pm. Confirm hours on the county page before you haul. County solid waste page Water and power Two numbers worth saving in your phone. Both utilities take outage calls around the clock. Water: San Lorenzo Valley Water District If your home is served by the district, start or stop service through the Start and Stop Service page . Give at least 24 business hours of notice, and expect a $20 establishment fee on the first bill. Accounts go in the property owner's name. Customer service and emergencies: 831-338-2153. After hours, the same number transfers to an answering service that reaches on-call staff, per the district's customer service page . Some properties in the area are on private wells or small mutual systems instead; your closing documents or neighbors can tell you which. Power: PG&E For a downed power line, stay away from it and anything it is touching, call 911, then call PG&E at 1-800-743-5000. To report an outage, use the PG&E Outage Center or call 1-800-743-5002. PG&E's general customer service line is 1-877-660-6789. All three numbers are on PG&E's report an emergency page . Sign up for outage alerts so shutoffs don't catch you off guard. If someone in your home depends on power for medical needs, the Medical Baseline Program adds a monthly energy allowance and extra notifications ahead of safety shutoffs. It's based on medical need, not income. Emergency readiness Set this up before you need it. This page points to official programs. It is not an alert service, and in an emergency you should call 911 and follow agency instructions. CruzAware alerts The county's official emergency alert registration. Choose calls, texts, or email. Every adult in the household should register their own phone. Sign up Boulder Creek Fire Protection District 13230 Central Avenue, office 831-338-7222. Call 911 for emergencies; use the office line for prevention questions and district business. BCFD site Defensible space California law requires 100 feet of defensible space around homes. The Fire Safe Council of Santa Cruz County breaks the work into zones and explains where to start. Zone guide Free chipping No-cost chipping is available to residents in high fire risk areas of the county, run by different providers depending on where you live. The Resource Conservation District covers most of the San Lorenzo Valley, with spring registration in April and a fall reimbursement option. Program windows change yearly, so check the current pages. Chipping programs Roads Know who maintains which road. Beyond Highways 9 and 236, which Caltrans maintains, a road may be county-maintained, privately maintained, or maintained through a road association or county service area. Check the Santa Cruz County road-maintenance map before assuming the county is responsible for a particular road. Permits and building Check before you build, dig, or cut. Mountain parcels come with septic, geologic, and tree rules that flatland owners never meet. A short call to the county early saves real money later. Building and zoning permits The county's Unified Permit Center, part of Community Development and Infrastructure , handles building, zoning, environmental, and public works permits for unincorporated areas like Boulder Creek. Permit Center Septic systems Most homes here are on septic. Visit Boulder Creek: Redwoods, Town and Local Guide 0 Come curious, come prepared Visit Boulder Creek A small mountain town at the north end of the San Lorenzo Valley, surrounded by redwoods. Plan ahead, drive for the roads, and leave room for weather and access to change. Confirm hours and conditions with each place before you go. Check conditions Find food and drink Getting here Plan the drive first. Boulder Creek sits on Highway 9. The roads in are winding and mostly two lanes, so give yourself extra time and check conditions before you leave. By car From Santa Cruz, take Highway 9 north up the valley through Felton and Ben Lomond. From the Santa Clara Valley side, Highway 9 climbs over the summit from Saratoga. A common alternative from Highway 17 is Bear Creek Road, which drops into Boulder Creek from the east. All three are slow mountain roads with tight curves, cyclists, and wildlife, so use pullouts to let faster traffic by. Check the roads Winter storms and summer roadwork both close lanes up here. Check Caltrans QuickMap for real-time closures and chain controls, and the County Road Closure Dashboard for local roads. Our Mountain Status page pulls together the same sources. Cell service is patchy along parts of Highway 9, so it helps to have directions saved before you lose signal. Riding the bus? Santa Cruz METRO Routes 35 and 35X connect Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley with Santa Cruz. The 35X is a weekday express; Route 35 covers nights and weekends. Check the current schedule with METRO before you plan a trip. The redwoods Parks and trails nearby. Access in these parks keeps changing after the 2020 CZU fire. Confirm hours, reservations, and open trails on each official page the day you go. Big Basin Redwoods State Park California's oldest state park is open for limited day-use as it recovers from the CZU fire, and much of it is still closed. Parking is limited and first come, first served. Reservations are encouraged, not required. As of July 16, 2026, the state lists day-use fees of $6 plus a $2 reservation fee, or $10 without a reservation, and no fee to arrive by foot, bike, or bus. There is no drinking water on site except at the kiosk. Confirm the current status before you drive up. Big Basin access, State Parks Castle Rock State Park Sandstone formations and ridge-top views along Skyline. It sits on Highway 35 about two and a half miles southeast of the Highway 9 junction. Parking is $10 a day at a self-serve kiosk, and the gate is locked at sunset. Weekdays are quieter for parking. Castle Rock, State Parks Fall Creek, Henry Cowell A quiet day-use unit with about twenty miles of trails through redwoods and old lime kilns. The trailhead and free parking are on Felton Empire Road off Highway 9. There are no facilities, and dogs, bikes, and fires are not allowed. Henry Cowell, State Parks Closer to town, the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District keeps up Junction Park , with a small beach, San Lorenzo River access, a lawn, and picnic tables one block off the main street. Barbara Day Park sits just downstream, and Garrahan Park up Highway 9 has a walking track, fields, and barbecue areas. The river beach at Junction Park is where Boulder Creek kids learn to swim, mine included, and it runs on the same arrangement it always has: little kids on the sand, bigger kids on the rocks, cold water for everyone. It's swim at your own risk. Choose your own adventure A perfect day in Boulder Creek. Five stops, three ways to make each one yours. This is the itinerary I give friends when they visit. Hours change up here, so check before you count on any single stop. Start with breakfast Jenna Sue's Coffee and a casual downtown start. The Tree House Cafe The other local coffee stop, made for lingering. Bella's Cafe The town's sit-down breakfast. Earn your lunch Play a round Nine holes under the redwoods at the Boulder Creek Golf and Country Club . Swim The rec district pool in season, or the river beach at Junction Park. Boulder Creek Mountain Status: Weather, Roads and Outages 0 Conditions and official links Mountain Status A quick starting point for weather, smoke, roads, outages, and emergency information affecting Boulder Creek. This is not an emergency alert service. For immediate danger, call 911. Confirm urgent information with the responsible agency. Live conditions Current mountain snapshot Live status is available below. Forecast, NWS alerts, optional AirNow data, cached fallbacks, and official source links update inside the embedded tool. Loading live conditions. If they do not appear, use the official sources below. How to read this page Every panel in the snapshot above is fetched from the agency that publishes it at the moment you open this page. Nothing is written ahead of time, nothing is cached overnight, and nothing here decides whether a road, a river, or the air is fine. Those calls belong to the agencies below, and in an emergency they belong to 911. Boulder Creek Local is a community guide, not an alert service. What this page does is put the official screens in one place and say plainly where each number came from, so you can reach the source in one click when it matters. What follows does not change from day to day: it is the map of the page, not a report on conditions. What each panel checks, and who publishes it Air quality. A modeled US AQI and PM2.5 estimate for downtown Boulder Creek from Open-Meteo . A model is not a monitor. During a smoke event the ground monitors on the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map are the ones to work from, and in a canyon they can differ from a modeled figure by a wide margin. Highway closures. The Caltrans District 5 lane closure feed, filtered to Santa Cruz County on Highways 1, 9, 17, 35, and 236. State highways only. County-maintained roads, including Bear Creek Road, Jamison Creek Road, and China Grade, are not in that feed at all. For those, use the Santa Cruz County road dashboard , and check Caltrans QuickMap for the state routes before you drive. San Lorenzo River. Gage height in feet and streamflow in cubic feet per second from USGS gauge 11160500, San Lorenzo River at Big Trees, in Felton. It is the nearest real-time gauge downstream of Boulder Creek, so it reads the valley rather than the town. The panel prints the reading, the time it was taken, and the National Weather Service stages published for forecast point BTEC1, and it stops there. Turning a reading into a flood call is the NWS river forecast 's job, not ours. Weather forecast and alerts. The National Weather Service API, queried for a single point, downtown Boulder Creek. Alerts are point specific: a warning in force over another part of Santa Cruz County may not appear here at all. The full county picture is at the NWS Bay Area office . Power. Direct links to the PG&E outage map, the outage alert signup for your address, and the report line. Boulder Creek Local does not read a PG&E feed and does not restate one. The outage map is the source. Sirens and smoke. Links to the same screens dispatchers feed. PulsePoint shows Boulder Creek Fire Protection District calls with the units responding. Watch Duty carries human-verified wildfire updates. The CAL FIRE incident list covers state incidents. The ALERTCalifornia cameras at Brookdale and Mt. Bielawski are steerable cameras for situational awareness. The CHP dispatch log lists highway incidents under the Monterey Communications Center, which covers Highways 9 and 236. The Sheriff's calls-for-service lookup is a records search by address, not a live feed. What these panels will not tell you Whether anything is safe. No panel converts a reading into advice. A number is published with its source and its timestamp, and the judgment stays with the agency that owns it. What is not being shown. An empty feed means not shown, not nothing happening. Law enforcement calls are generally not published live anywhere public, and several incident types are excluded from the Sheriff's lookup by policy. Evacuation information. Zones, warnings, and orders come from CruzAware and from the agency issuing them. That is the one thing this page will never summarize, paraphrase, or delay. A reading you can rely on later. Each panel is read once, when the page loads, and the timestamp on the snapshot says so. Reload to read it again. If what you see here disagrees with an agency's own page, the agency is right. Final numbers. USGS river data arrives provisional and is revised afterward. The panel labels it that way for a reason. When a panel says unavailable Unavailable means the feed did not answer, or answered with something the page could not read. It never means the condition is fine. Missing data is missing, and the useful response is to go straight to the source. Air quality unavailable: AirNow Fire and Smoke Map . Roads unavailable: Caltrans QuickMap for state highways, the county road dashboard for county roads. River unavailable: the USGS gauge page and the NWS river forecast . Weather unavailable: the NWS Bay Area office and its Boulder Creek point forecast. Anything involving fire or smoke: Watch Duty and the CAL FIRE incident list , with CruzAware for anything that becomes an order. Three numbers worth keeping in your phone. Report a power outage to PG&E at 1-800-743-5002 . For a downed power line, call 911 first, then PG&E at 1-800-743-5000 . For a tree or a slide on a county-maintained road, Santa Cruz County road dispatch is 831-477-3999 . Questions we get Is this an official alert service? No. Boulder Creek Local is an independent community guide with no dispatch role and no standing with any agency. Official alerts for Santa Cruz County come through CruzAware , which takes a few minutes to sign up for and is the most useful link on this page. Emergencies go to 911. Why does the page not just say whether Highway 9 is passable? Because the feed cannot hold that sentence up. Caltrans publishes lane closures on its own schedule, so a closure that started minutes ago may not be in the data yet, and a county road closure will never be in it. A page that printed an all clear would be guessing, and guessing about a mountain road is how somebody ends up driving into one. My road is not a state highway. Where do I look? The county road dashboard covers county-maintained roads, and Santa Cruz County road dispatch takes reports at 831-477-3999 . Private roads and shared driveways belong to their owners or road associations, which is worth knowing before a storm rather than during one. The air quality figure here does not match the app on my phone. Which is right? They measure different things. The panel above is a model, an estimate built from regional conditions for a point in Boulder Creek. Most phone apps blend monitors, and smoke apps read sensors directly. When smoke is the question, use the ground monitors on the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map and treat the modeled number as background context. What is gage height, and is a given reading high? Gage height is the height of the water surface above the gauge's own reference point. It is not the depth of the river and it is not comparable between gauges. Streamflow, in cubic feet per second, is the volume moving past the gauge. Whether a reading matters is answered by the National Weather Service stages for that gauge, published on the NWS river forecast page . The panel quotes those stages with attribution and does not invent its own. I heard sirens. How do I find out what that was? Start with PulsePoint for fire and medical calls in the Boulder Creek Fire Protection District, then the CHP dispatch log for highway collisions and Watch Duty for anything that looks like wildfire. Law enforcement calls are generally not visible in real time, so a screen with nothing on it is not an answer to what you heard. How often does this page update? Every time you load it. There is no overnight refresh and no stored copy of a previous reading. That is also why the snapshot carries the time it was retrieved: it is telling you how old the data on your screen already is. Can Boulder Creek Local text me when something happens? No, and we would not want to sit between you and an evacuation order. Sign up with CruzAware for county alerts, PG&E outage alerts for your address, and the PulsePoint Respond and Watch Duty apps for calls and wildfire. Those come from the agencies themselves, with no extra link in the chain. Jobs in Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley 0 Work nearby Jobs in the San Lorenzo Valley The board carries three kinds of work, and it helps to know which is which before you start scrolling. Inside the valley, openings are scarce, and most of them come from San Lorenzo Valley Unified. The district is the largest employer up here by a wide margin, and its instructional assistant, coaching and substitute positions turn over through the year. Within commuting distance there's a good deal more: the county's other school districts, the County Office of Education, Cabrillo College, city and county agencies, and retail and hospitality in Santa Cruz, Scotts Valley, Aptos and Capitola. These show an estimated drive time on each card, and anything genuinely far, like Watsonville, is marked as an extended commute and kept off the local tab unless you ask for it. Remote roles open to people in California sit on their own tab. The board refreshes each morning, and the date it last ran is at the top, so you can see how current it is. Before you take the on-site job Santa Cruz is about 30 minutes from Boulder Creek on a clear day and considerably longer when Highway 9 is wet, dark, or closed. San Jose is roughly the same 30 minutes over Bear Creek Road, in good conditions and can be twice that at commute times. Winter storms close Highway 9 more often than newcomers expect, and a closure turns a short drive into a long detour through Felton or over the summit. None of that makes a commute a bad idea. Plenty of people here do it happily. It's worth driving the route at the hour you'd actually be driving it before you commit to it. What this board doesn't have A lot of valley work never gets posted anywhere. Trades, caregiving, cleaning, landscaping, seasonal help and shop shifts are usually filled by word of mouth or a sign in a window. For that kind of work the directory is a better starting point than any job board: find the businesses you'd want to work for, and ask them directly. Listings link back to wherever the job was posted. For school and remote roles that's usually a job board, EDJOIN for the districts and We Work Remotely or Remotive for remote work. City and county agencies, and larger employers, more often link to their own application system. Boulder Creek Local isn't the employer and doesn't handle applications, so confirm the details at the source before you apply. Rentals in Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley 0 Places to live Rentals in the San Lorenzo Valley This is a small board, and it usually will be. The valley has very little rental stock, a good share of it changes hands privately, and what does get listed tends to go quickly. A short list here isn't a sign the board is broken. It's an accurate picture of a thin market. Listings cover long-term rentals in Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, Brookdale and Felton, drawn from property managers and public listings. Each one shows when it was last confirmed, so you can tell a fresh listing from a stale one, and each links back to its original source. The board refreshes each morning, and the date it last ran is shown at the top. Before you send anyone money Never wire money, send a deposit, or pay an application fee before you've seen the place in person and confirmed who you're dealing with. Rental scams follow tight markets, and this is one. A listing that pressures you to pay quickly, or asks you to pay before viewing, is a listing to walk away from. Boulder Creek Local isn't the landlord, the property manager, or a party to any agreement. We publish what's listed publicly, and we can be wrong. The rest of the market Because so much of the valley's renting happens outside listing sites, people who find places here usually do it by being visible locally: the community boards on Facebook, a note at the market, telling neighbors you're looking. Most valley rentals are filled before they're ever advertised, and that matches what turns up on this board. If you're new to the area, Resident Resources covers what to sort out once you land: water, power, trash, internet, and what living on a septic system and a mountain road actually involves. The local letter Useful local information, gathered with care. About Boulder Creek Local 0 About the project Built by a local who got tired of ten tabs. Boulder Creek Local exists to make dependable local information easy to find, easy to trust, and easy to keep current. Why this exists It started with a childcare search. When our baby arrived and my return to work started counting down, I went looking for infant care and found almost nothing to look at. The valley's providers are real, and some are wonderful, but most have no website and no active social media, so as far as the internet is concerned they barely exist. I found our spot the old mountain way: through word of mouth, one recommendation at a time, while the clock ran. Somewhere in those conversations it clicked that this valley solves most of its problems the same way, and that somebody should start writing the answers down. This site is me writing the answers down. Who's behind it Born here. Still here. I'm Adrienne. I was born and raised in Boulder Creek and never really left: my partner and I are raising our family here on a small homestead with chickens, ducks, one opinionated goose named Lucy, dogs, cats, and a garden that wins some years and loses others. I've swum in the river at Junction Park since before I could ride a bike, and these days I get to watch the next generation discover the same sandy beach. I believe in shopping local and in the businesses that keep a small town running, and I believe information about this town should be as easy to find as the town is easy to love. The mission Reduce friction. Strengthen local connection. Residents shouldn't need ten tabs to check conditions , find a service , or learn what's happening . Visitors should have enough context to arrive prepared and respectful. 01 Useful first Every page should help someone answer a real question or take a clear next step. 02 Source-aware Time-sensitive information points back to the responsible agency or organizer, with the date we checked it. 03 Open to correction Local information changes. There's always a simple way to flag an update, and corrections make the site better. Independence Listings are not endorsements. Nobody pays to be listed here, and nobody can pay their way out of a correction. Boulder Creek Local may eventually support itself through clearly labeled sponsorships, commerce, or services. Paid relationships will not quietly determine factual status information or correction decisions. Questions, corrections, and story tips: hello@bouldercreeklocal.com .
